topic.title: Similar 2D shapes: length and area ratios; effect of enlargement on volume
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One question in most series, 1 to 4 marks, very often the last question on the paper; it appears in M7 and again in M8, which re-examines M7 content. Summer 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q14 (1 + 1, perimeter then area after an enlargement, repeated as M8 Paper 1 Q5); Summer 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q9 (1 + 1, a ratio of areas to a ratio of heights and then of volumes); November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q13 (2, a side in similar triangles, MA1 A1); Summer 2023 M8 Paper 1 Q9 (2, the volume after the height is doubled, M1 A1); Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q16 (3, a ratio of areas to a length, MA1 MA1 A1); November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q16 and M8 Paper 2 Q8 (4, two areas and heights x and x + a, working demanded).
mustMemorise: Length scale factor k → area scale factor k² → volume scale factor k³
Backwards: k = √(area factor), k = ∛(volume factor); take the root before the factor touches a length
Perimeter is a length, so it scales by k
Similar: equal corresponding angles and all corresponding sides in the same ratio
In a triangle with a line drawn parallel to one side, the side matching AD is the whole of AB, never the leftover DB
notOnThisSpec: Similar 3-D solids in their own right (surface-area and volume ratios of similar solids, including the frustum of a cone) — that is M8-GM-05 and has its own topic
Formal similarity proofs quoting SSS, SAS or AAA criteria
Congruence criteria as a named list (M6)
Any scale factor for an angle: angles are unchanged by an enlargement

note.title: Similar shapes: k, k² and k³
note.subject: maths

given: Nothing for this topic. The Higher sheet carries the prism, the trapezium, the sphere, the cone, the quadratic formula, the sine and cosine rules and ½ab sin C — no scale-factor rule appears on it.
mustKnow: Length scale factor k → area scale factor k² → volume scale factor k³
Backwards: k = √(area factor) and k = ∛(volume factor)
Perimeter is a length, so it scales by k, not by k²
Similar means equal angles and every pair of corresponding sides in the same ratio
A ratio a : b of lengths gives a² : b² for areas and a³ : b³ for volumes

notOnThisSpec: Similar 3-D solids in their own right — surface-area and volume ratios of similar solids, including the frustum of a cone, are statement M8-GM-05 and have their own topic (similar-3d-shapes-length-area-and-volume-ratios)

Formal similarity proofs written as a two-column geometric proof; CCEA asks you to show that corresponding angles are equal or that sides are in a fixed ratio, not to quote SSS/SAS similarity criteria
Congruence criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) as a named list — congruence is M6 and is treated as the k = 1 case here
Scale factors applied to angles: angles never change under enlargement, so there is no angle scale factor to find

mustBeAbleTo: Say what makes two shapes similar: equal angles, and every pair of corresponding sides in the same ratio
Find the length scale factor k by pairing corresponding sides and dividing the right way round
Multiply a length, a height or a perimeter by k
Multiply an area by k² and a volume by k³, and say which of the three you are being asked for
Go backwards from an area ratio to a length ratio by taking the square root of both parts
Go backwards from a volume ratio to a length ratio by taking the cube root of both parts
Run the whole chain in one question: an area ratio to the lengths, then the lengths to the volumes
Pick out a pair of similar triangles inside one diagram when a line is drawn parallel to a side, and match the whole of a side with the whole of a side
Turn a percentage increase in area into a percentage increase in length, and the reverse
Set up and solve an equation when the two heights are given as x and x + something
Do all of it without a calculator on Paper 1: simplify the ratio first, then take the root of two small numbers
sheet.howExamined: M7 Paper 1 and Paper 2 (each non-calculator/calculator, 75 minutes, 50 marks) and again in M8, which re-examines M7 content. Expect one question, very often the last on the paper, 1 to 4 marks. The shapes seen: two single-mark parts asking how many times bigger the perimeter and the area become after an enlargement (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q14, repeated as M8 Paper 1 Q5); a 1 + 1 pair taking a ratio of surface areas to a ratio of heights and then to a ratio of volumes (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q9); a 2-mark similar-triangles side (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q13, scheme MA1 A1); a 2-mark volume after the height is doubled (Summer 2023 M8 Paper 1 Q9, scheme M1 A1); a 3-mark area-ratio-to-length (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q16, scheme MA1 MA1 A1); and a 4-mark version where the two heights are x and x + k and the working must be shown (November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q16 and M8 Paper 2 Q8). Marks run MA1 for the simplified ratio, MA1 for the root, A1 for the value.
traps: Using the area scale factor as if it were the length scale factor — the single biggest loss on this topic; the factor 4 was found from a 24 : 96 area ratio and then divided into the length, giving 15 ÷ 4 instead of 15 ÷ 2 (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q16)
Multiplying a volume by k instead of k³: most candidates doubled the volume when the height was doubled, where only the stronger ones multiplied by 8 (Summer 2023 M8 Paper 1 Q9)
Stopping at the area ratio: one mark for 1 : 16 was common, but the step down to heights 1 : 4 was rarely made, so x = 3 was reached by very few (November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q16)
Giving the same answer for perimeter and for area after an enlargement — 5 was written twice, and 10 was a common area answer for a scale factor of 5 (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 1 Q14)
Subtracting instead of scaling in similar triangles: 10 − 4 = 6, so 15 − 6 (November 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q13)
Writing the right answer with no working where the question says to show it, which scores nothing (November 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q8)
Pairing a part of a side with the whole of a side when the two triangles overlap: AD : DB instead of AD : AB
Dividing the wrong way round, so a shape that should grow shrinks; check the answer is on the correct side of the one you started from

workedExamples.stem:
Triangles $A$ and $B$ are similar.

The base of $A$ is 4 cm and the base of $B$ is 10 cm.
The area of $A$ is 22 cm².

Work out the area of $B$.

steps.decision: The two bases are corresponding sides, so dividing one by the other gives the length scale factor. I put $B$ on top because $B$ is the shape I am moving to, which keeps $k$ greater than 1 and means the area must come out larger. I leave it as a fraction: this is Paper 1.
The question asks for an **area**, so the factor is squared. An area is a length times a length, and both of those lengths have been multiplied by $k$.

options: Because an area is a length times a length, so two factors of k arrive
Because every scale factor is squared before it is used
Because the shapes are triangles and triangles use one half base times height
whyMenu.explain: Two dimensions, two factors of $k$. A perimeter would take one, a volume three. Counting dimensions is what tells you which power to use.

steps.decision: Multiplying by the fraction is safer by hand than converting to 6.25 first: 22 × 25 is a short multiplication and dividing by 4 at the end is two halvings.

steps.working: $= 137.5$, so the area of $B$ is 137.5 cm².
steps.decision: 550 ÷ 4 = 137.5. The answer line has no unit printed on it, so I write cm² myself — an area answer given in cm loses the accuracy mark.

twin.stem: $P$ and $Q$ are similar triangles. The base of $P$ is 6 cm and the base of $Q$ is 15 cm. The area of $P$ is 28 cm². Work out the area of $Q$.

workedExamples.stem:
Two similar tiles $P$ and $Q$ are shown.

The area of $P$ is 45 cm² and the area of $Q$ is 125 cm².
The longest edge of $Q$ is 20 cm.

Work out the length of the longest edge of $P$.

steps.decision: Simplify before doing anything else. Both numbers divide by 5, and 9 : 25 is a pair of square numbers, which is the signal that the root is about to be clean. In every CCEA scheme for this topic, this simplified ratio is the first mark.
Areas carry $k^2$, so the square root takes me back to $k$. This is the step the examiners report as the one candidates miss — they use the area factor directly on a length.

options: Because the area ratio is the length ratio squared, so rooting both parts undoes it
Because you always halve a ratio before using it
Because the tiles are quadrilaterals, so the ratio has four parts
whyMenu.explain: $3 : 5$ squared is $9 : 25$, so rooting is exactly the way back. Halving would give $4.5 : 12.5$, which is the same ratio and no help at all.

steps.decision: $P$ is the smaller tile, so I multiply by $\tfrac{3}{5}$ and the answer must come out below 20. Checking that direction takes a second and catches an upside-down scale factor.

twin.stem: Two similar shapes have areas 8 cm² and 98 cm². The height of the larger shape is 21 cm. Work out the height of the smaller shape.

workedExamples.stem:
Two similar cylinders $C$ and $D$ are shown.

The ratio of the curved surface area of $C$ to the curved surface area of $D$ is $4 : 25$.

(a) Write down the ratio of the height of $C$ to the height of $D$.
(b) The volume of $C$ is 48 cm³. Work out the volume of $D$.

steps.decision: Surface area is an area, so it carries $k^2$. Square-rooting each part of the ratio brings me back to the lengths. Part (a) is one mark for exactly this line.
Now cube the **length** ratio, not the area ratio. There is no direct route from areas to volumes; the lengths are the bridge, and writing both lines is what earns both marks.

options: Because the length ratio cubed gives the volume ratio
Because the area ratio cubed gives the volume ratio
Because volumes and areas are always in the same ratio
whyMenu.explain: Cubing the area ratio would give $64 : 15625$, which is $k^6$, not $k^3$. Land on the lengths first, every time.

steps.decision: The ratio $8 : 125$ means $C$ is 8 parts. Dividing the known volume by 8 gives the size of one part, which is the standard way to use a ratio when one side is known.
Multiply the size of one part by $D$'s 125 parts. The unit is cm³ because it is a volume — and a volume answer left in cm² is treated as an error of accuracy.

twin.stem: The ratio of the surface areas of two similar boxes is $9 : 16$. The volume of the smaller box is 54 cm³. Work out the volume of the larger box.

steps.decision: Both triangles share the apex $P$, so the side of the large triangle that matches $PS$ is the **whole** of $PQ$, not the leftover piece $SQ$. Adding the two parts first is what stops the commonest mismatch on this topic.

$ST$ is parallel to $QR$, so the corresponding angles are equal and the apex angle is shared: the triangles are similar. Dividing the whole by the part gives the factor that takes the small triangle to the large one.

options: Because PS and PQ are corresponding sides, both measured from the shared apex P
Because SQ is the part left over, so SQ divided by PS is the scale factor
Because ST and SQ are corresponding sides
whyMenu.explain: Using $\tfrac{8}{12} = 0.666667$ would treat the leftover piece as a whole side. Every answer after that is out, even though the method looks right.

steps.decision: $ST$ and $QR$ are the corresponding parallel sides, so a single factor of $k$ takes one to the other. Length, so $k$ to the power 1.
$TR$ is not a side of either triangle, so I scale the whole side $PR$ first and subtract the part I already know. Answering 25 here would be answering a question that was not asked.

twin.stem: In triangle $ABC$, $D$ lies on $AB$ and $E$ lies on $AC$, with $DE$ parallel to $BC$. $AD = 10$ cm, $DB = 5$ cm and $DE = 14$ cm. Work out the length of $BC$.

items.skill: Area scale factor from a length scale factor
items.stem: A shape is enlarged by scale factor 4. How many times bigger is its area?

options.feedback: $4^2 = 16$. Two dimensions, two factors of $k$, and one mark in the exam for one line.
That is what happens to a **length** — a side, a height, the perimeter. An area takes $k$ twice.
That is $4$ doubled. Squaring and doubling agree only at 2, which is why this slip survives so long.
$4^3$ is the **volume** factor. An area is flat, so it takes two factors of $k$, not three.

items.skill: Volume scale factor from a length scale factor
items.stem: A solid is enlarged by scale factor 3. How many times bigger is its volume?

options.feedback: $3^3 = 27$. Three dimensions, three factors of $k$.
$3^2$ is the surface-area factor. The solid has a third dimension as well.
Scaling the volume by $k$ alone is the error the Summer 2023 report names: the majority multiplied the volume by the length factor.
That is $3$ doubled. A cube is $3 \times 3 \times 3$.

items.skill: Area ratio back to a length ratio
items.stem: Two similar shapes have areas in the ratio $1 : 36$. What is the ratio of their lengths?

options.feedback: $\sqrt{36} = 6$. Root both parts and the areas become lengths.
That is the area ratio copied across. It is the single biggest mark-loser on this topic; the root has to happen before the ratio touches a length.
Halving is not the inverse of squaring. $18^2 = 324$, nowhere near 36.
That squares again, moving further from the lengths. To undo a square you take a square root.

items.skill: Volume ratio back to a length ratio
items.stem: Two similar solids have volumes in the ratio $1 : 64$. What is the ratio of their heights?

options.feedback: $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$, because $4^3 = 64$. Volumes need the cube root.
That is the square root. It would be right for a ratio of areas; a ratio of volumes carries $k^3$, so the cube root is the way back.
The volume ratio used unchanged on a length. Check it: heights $1 : 64$ would give volumes $1 : 262144$.
Halving undoes doubling, not cubing. $32^3 = 32768$.

items.stem: Triangles $A$ and $B$ are similar. Work out the length marked $x$, in cm.

options.feedback: That adds the difference $15 - 6 = 9$. Similar shapes scale by multiplying; the November 2024 report saw exactly this subtraction.
The scale factor has been used upside down, so the larger triangle came out smaller. Check the direction before you divide.
The sides have been paired the other way round, matching $8$ cm with the base instead of with its own partner. Pair first, divide second.

items.stem: A cone has volume 20 cm³. A similar cone is made with 3 times the height. What is its volume, in cm³?

options.feedback: $20 \times 3^3 = 20 \times 27 = 540$ cm³.
The volume has been multiplied by the length factor. The width and the depth grew by $3$ as well, so the cube is what is needed.
$3^2$ is the surface-area factor. A volume takes the third power.
Adding 3 treats the scale factor as a length to add on. It is a multiplier.

items.stem: A shape has perimeter 12 cm. It is enlarged by scale factor 3. What is the new perimeter, in cm?

options.feedback: A perimeter is a sum of lengths, so it scales by $k$: $12 \times 3 = 36$ cm.
$k^2$ belongs to the area. Summer 2025 examiners saw the same factor used for both; only the area is squared.
The scale factor has been added rather than multiplied.
Dividing shrinks the shape. An enlargement by a factor above 1 makes the perimeter longer.

items.skill: Which line earns the first mark
items.stem: Two similar shapes have areas 12 cm² and 108 cm². Their heights are $x$ cm and $(x + 8)$ cm, and the part is worth 4 marks with the working to be shown. Which first line earns the first mark?

options.feedback: The simplified area ratio is the mark almost everyone can get, and it is the line every scheme for this topic opens with.
The area factor has jumped straight into an equation about heights. The lengths are in the ratio $1 : 3$, not $1 : 9$.
The value is right, and with the working demanded it scores nothing on its own. November 2025 examiners reported precisely this.
A difference between two areas is not a scale factor. Similar shapes are linked by multiplying.

parts.stem:
A shape is enlarged by scale factor 6.

Write down how many times bigger the area of the shape becomes.
hints: An area is a length multiplied by a length.
Both of those lengths grow by 6.
parts.workedSolution: Area takes two factors of $k$, so the area factor is $6^2 = 36$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the factor for a length or a perimeter. An area needs $k$ twice. Summer 2025 examiners saw the same number written for both parts of exactly this question.
That is $6$ doubled rather than squared. Doubling and squaring only agree at 2.
$6^3$ is the volume factor. A flat shape has two dimensions, so the power is 2.

parts.stem:
A solid is enlarged by scale factor 6.

Write down how many times bigger the volume of the solid becomes.
hints: A volume is a length multiplied by a length multiplied by a length.
All three grow by 6.
parts.workedSolution: Volume takes three factors of $k$, so the volume factor is $6^3 = 216$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the length factor. The solid grew in three directions at once, so the volume factor is the cube. This is the error the Summer 2023 report says the majority of candidates made.
$6^2$ is the surface-area factor. A solid has a third dimension too.
That is $6$ trebled rather than cubed.

emphasis: area ratio back to a length ratio

parts.stem:
The area of shape $B$ is 121 times the area of the similar shape $A$.

Write down the length scale factor from $A$ to $B$.
hints: Take the square root.

commonErrors.feedback: The area factor has been copied across to the lengths. It is $k^2$: root it first. This one step is what the Summer 2024 report found candidates missing.
Halving does not undo squaring. Check it: $60.5^2 = 3660.25$.

context.setting: Two similar rectangles on a printed sheet

parts.stem:
$A$ and $B$ are similar rectangles.

$A$ has length 5 cm and area 12 cm².
$B$ has length 20 cm.

Work out the area of $B$.
hints: Pair the two lengths: $20 \div 5$.
You are asked for an area, so square the factor.
Give the answer in cm².
parts.workedSolution: $k = 20 \div 5 = 4$, so $k^2 = 16$ and the area of $B$ is $12 \times 16 = 192$ cm².

commonErrors.feedback: The length factor 4 has been used on an area. Square it first: the area factor is 16.
That cubes the factor, which is what a volume would need. A rectangle is flat.

The larger one is labelled as the new box with its volume marked as unknown, and a note says every length is 3 times as long. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
A storage box is a cuboid of volume 45 cm³.

A similar box is made in which every length is 3 times as long.

Work out the volume of the new box.
hints: The box grew in three directions, not one.
Volume factor $= 3^3$.
Give the answer in cm³.
parts.workedSolution: The volume factor is $3^3 = 27$, so the new volume is $45 \times 27 = 1215$ cm³.

commonErrors.feedback: The volume has been multiplied by the length factor. The box is 3 times longer, 3 times wider and 3 times taller, which is the cube. The Summer 2023 report records most candidates doing exactly this.
Squaring gives the surface-area factor. A volume takes the third power.

emphasis: volume ratio back to a length ratio

context.setting: Two similar solid models, no context

parts.stem:
Two similar solids have volumes 5 cm³ and 320 cm³.

Work out the length scale factor from the smaller solid to the larger solid.
hints: Divide to find how many times bigger the volume is.
That number is $k^3$.
Take the cube root: which number cubed gives 64?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the square root. A volume ratio carries $k^3$, so the cube root is the way back; the square root would be right for a ratio of areas.
64 is how many times bigger the **volume** is. MA1 is yours for finding it; the length factor is its cube root.

context.setting: Two similar shapes with their areas given

figures.alt: Two similar shapes drawn as triangles. Shape A has area 18 square centimetres and its height marked as unknown. Shape B is larger, with area 162 square centimetres and height 21 cm. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
Shapes $A$ and $B$ are similar.

The area of $A$ is 18 cm² and the area of $B$ is 162 cm².
The height of $B$ is 21 cm.

Work out the height of $A$.

scheme.examinerNote: Follow through a candidate's own area ratio into its square root.

hints: Write the two areas as a ratio and simplify it.
Square-root both parts to reach the heights.
$B$ is the larger shape, so $A$'s height is smaller than 21 cm.
parts.workedSolution: Areas $18 : 162 = 1 : 9$. Heights $= 1 : \sqrt{9} = 1 : 3$. So the height of $A$ is $21 \div 3 = 7$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The area factor 9 has been divided into the height. MA1 is yours for finding it, and one square root turns it into the 3 the height actually needs. This is the Summer 2024 question almost exactly.
The factor has been used upside down, so the smaller shape came out taller than the larger one. Check the direction before dividing.

context.setting: Two similar triangles printed side by side

figures.alt: Two similar triangles. Triangle A has its base marked 9 cm and the side above it marked 12 cm. Triangle B is larger, with its base marked 15 cm and the corresponding side marked x cm. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
Triangles $A$ and $B$ are similar.

The base of $A$ is 9 cm and the base of $B$ is 15 cm.
The side marked on $A$ is 12 cm.

Work out the length marked $x$.
hints: The two bases correspond, so they give $k$.
$B$ is the larger triangle, so $x$ is more than 12 cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The difference $15 - 9 = 6$ has been added on. Similar shapes are linked by a multiplier; the November 2024 report describes the same subtraction.
The scale factor has been used upside down, so the larger triangle came out with the shorter side.
The 12 cm side has been paired with a base rather than with its own partner. Pair first, then divide.

figures.alt: Two similar cones standing on their bases, drawn as paper cups. The small cup has height 8 cm and holds 35 cubic centimetres. The large cup has height 20 cm and its capacity is marked as unknown. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
Two paper cups are similar cones.

The small cup is 8 cm high and holds 35 cm³.
The large cup is 20 cm high.

Calculate how much the large cup holds.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Heights correspond, so they give $k$.
Capacity is a volume, so cube $k$.
Round only at the end, to 3 significant figures.
parts.workedSolution: $k = 20 \div 8 = 2.5$, so $k^3 = 15.625$. The large cup holds $35 \times 15.625 = 546.875$ cm³, which is 547 cm³ to 3 significant figures.

commonErrors.feedback: The capacity has been multiplied by 2.5 rather than by 2.5³. MA1 is yours for the scale factor; the cube is the second mark.
Squaring gives the surface-area factor, which would be right for the paper the cup is made of, not for what it holds.

context.setting: Two similar solid shapes labelled A and B

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 480 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M78 118V196A32 12 0 0 0 142 196V118' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.05' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><ellipse cx='110' cy='118' rx='32' ry='12' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='110' y='224' text-anchor='middle' font-family='inherit' font-size='13' fill='currentColor' font-weight='600'>A</text><path d='M252 58V175A48 18 0 0 0 348 175V58' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.05' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><ellipse cx='300' cy='58' rx='48' ry='18' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='300' y='224' text-anchor='middle' font-family='inherit' font-size='13' fill='currentColor' font-weight='600'>B</text><text x='110' y='205' text-anchor='middle' font-family='inherit' font-size='12' fill='currentColor'>surface area 9 parts</text><text x='300' y='205' text-anchor='middle' font-family='inherit' font-size='12' fill='currentColor'>surface area 49 parts</text><text x='20' y='26' text-anchor='start' font-family='inherit' font-size='12.5' fill='currentColor'>Surface areas in the ratio 9 : 49</text><text x='464' y='240' text-anchor='end' font-family='inherit' font-size='10.5' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.7'>diagram not drawn accurately</text></svg>
figures.alt: Two similar solids drawn as cylinders. The smaller is labelled A and the larger is labelled B, and a note above them says the ratio of their surface areas is 9 : 49. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
$A$ and $B$ are similar solids.

Their surface areas are in the ratio $9 : 49$.

Write down the ratio of $A$'s height to $B$'s height.
hints: Surface area is an area, so it carries $k^2$.
Square-root each part of the ratio.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the area ratio written out again. Take the square root of each part to reach the heights — the step the Summer 2025 report says only the stronger candidates made.

parts.stem: Write down the ratio of $A$'s volume to $B$'s volume.

scheme.examinerNote: Follow through the candidate's own height ratio cubed.

hints: Cube each part of the height ratio from part (a).

commonErrors.feedback: The **area** ratio has been cubed. Cube the height ratio from part (a) instead; going straight from areas to volumes skips the lengths and raises $k$ to the sixth power.

parts.stem:
Two bottles of cordial are similar in shape.

The small bottle holds 250 ml and is 12 cm tall.
The large bottle holds 1500 ml.

Calculate the height of the large bottle.
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: How many times more does the large bottle hold?
That number is $k^3$, so take the cube root.
Keep the full cube root on your calculator and round only at the end.
parts.workedSolution: $1500 \div 250 = 6$, which is $k^3$. So $k = \sqrt[3]{6} = 1.81712\ldots$ and the height is $12 \times 1.81712\ldots = 21.8$ cm to 3 significant figures.

commonErrors.feedback: The square root has been used where the cube root is needed. Areas carry $k^2$; volumes carry $k^3$.
The volume factor 6 has been used on a height. MA1 is yours for finding it; it still has to be cube-rooted.

context.setting: Two similar photographs enlarged for a display

parts.stem:
Two photographs are similar rectangles.

The area of the larger photograph is 44% greater than the area of the smaller one.

Work out the percentage by which the width of the larger photograph is greater than the width of the smaller one.
The answer line is printed in %.
hints: "44% greater" means the area is multiplied by 1.44.
That multiplier is $k^2$.
Turn $k$ back into a percentage increase by subtracting 1.
parts.workedSolution: The area factor is $1 + 0.44 = 1.44$, and this is $k^2$. So $k = \sqrt{1.44} = 1.2$, which is an increase of 20%.

commonErrors.feedback: The area's percentage has been copied to the width. Convert to a multiplier, square-root it, then convert back.
Halving the percentage is not the same as square-rooting the multiplier: $1.22^2 = 1.4884$, not 1.44.

figures.alt: Two similar four-sided shapes. Shape A has area 8 square centimetres and height x cm. Shape B is larger, with area 98 square centimetres and height x plus 10 cm. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
Shapes $A$ and $B$ are similar.

The area of $A$ is 8 cm² and the area of $B$ is 98 cm².
The height of $A$ is $x$ cm and the height of $B$ is $(x + 10)$ cm.

Work out the value of $x$, showing your working clearly.

scheme.examinerNote: A correct value with no working scores zero here: the part demands the working.

hints: Simplify $8 : 98$ first — both parts divide by 2.
Square-root each part to get the heights.
Then $\dfrac{x}{x + 10} = \dfrac{2}{7}$, and cross-multiply.
parts.workedSolution: Areas $8 : 98 = 4 : 49$, so heights $= 2 : 7$. Then $\dfrac{x}{x + 10} = \dfrac{2}{7}$, so $7x = 2(x + 10) = 2x + 20$. That gives $5x = 20$ and $x = 4$. Check: the heights are 4 cm and 14 cm, in the ratio 2 : 7.

commonErrors.feedback: The area ratio 4 : 49 has been used as the height ratio. MA1 is yours for the ratio; square-root it before it goes into the equation. November 2025 examiners reported that this step was the one candidates could not make.

If the value is right but nothing else is on the page, the part scores nothing — it says to show the working clearly. Write the area ratio, the height ratio and the equation, and those marks are yours even if the final line slips.

parts.stem:
In the diagram, $S$ lies on $PQ$ and $T$ lies on $PR$, and $ST$ is parallel to $QR$.

$PS = 8$ cm, $SQ = 12$ cm and $ST = 14$ cm.

Work out the length of $QR$.
hints: Both triangles have their apex at $P$.
The side matching $PS$ is the whole of $PQ$, so add $8 + 12$ first.
$ST$ and $QR$ are the corresponding parallel sides.
parts.workedSolution: $ST$ is parallel to $QR$, so triangles $PST$ and $PQR$ are similar. $PQ = 8 + 12 = 20$ cm, so $k = 20 \div 8 = 2.5$ and $QR = 14 \times 2.5 = 35$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: $SQ$ has been paired with $PS$. $SQ$ is only the part of $PQ$ left over; the side that corresponds to $PS$ is the whole of $PQ$.
$SQ$ has been added to $ST$. Similar triangles scale by multiplying, not by adding a difference.

parts.stem:
Write down the ratio of the area of triangle $PST$ to the area of triangle $PQR$.

Give your ratio in its simplest form.
hints: The lengths are in the ratio $8 : 20$; simplify it.
Square each part of the length ratio.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the ratio of the lengths. Areas take the square of each part, so it becomes 4 : 25. Summer 2025 examiners saw the same number given for a length and for an area.

figures.alt: Two similar cylindrical tins standing upright. The smaller is labelled C with volume 128 cubic centimetres; the larger is labelled D with its volume marked as unknown. A note says the ratio of their curved surface areas is 16 : 81. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
$C$ and $D$ are similar cylindrical tins.

The ratio of the curved surface area of $C$ to the curved surface area of $D$ is $16 : 81$.

Write down the ratio of the height of $C$ to the height of $D$.
hints: Both 16 and 81 are square numbers.
Square-root each part.

commonErrors.feedback: The area ratio has been repeated. Square-root each part: a surface area carries $k^2$.

parts.stem: Work out the ratio of the volume of $C$ to the volume of $D$.
hints: Cube each part of your height ratio.

commonErrors.feedback: The area ratio has been cubed instead of the height ratio. Areas reach volumes only through the lengths.

parts.stem:
The volume of $C$ is 128 cm³.

Work out the volume of $D$.
hints: Your ratio says $C$ is 64 parts and $D$ is 729 parts.
Divide 128 by 64 to find one part.
Then multiply by 729.
parts.workedSolution: From part (b) the volumes are in the ratio $64 : 729$. One part is $128 \div 64 = 2$ cm³, so the volume of $D$ is $2 \times 729 = 1458$ cm³.

commonErrors.feedback: The **height** ratio has been used on a volume. Use the cubed ratio from part (b).
The area ratio has been used on a volume. The volumes are in the ratio 64 : 729.

figures.alt: Two similar cartons drawn as cuboids. The small carton has a label of area 60 square centimetres and holds 400 millilitres. The large carton has a label of area 135 square centimetres and its capacity is marked as unknown. The diagram is not drawn accurately.

parts.stem:
Two cartons of apple juice are similar.

The label on the small carton has area 60 cm² and the label on the large carton has area 135 cm².

Show that the ratio of the height of the small carton to the height of the large carton is $2 : 3$.

accepted: 60 : 135 = 4 : 9, and the square root of each part gives 2 : 3

scheme.examinerNote: The printed result is given, so the marks are for the chain above it, not for restating it.

hints: Simplify $60 : 135$ — both divide by 15.
A label is an area, so it carries $k^2$.
Square-root each part and the printed ratio appears.
parts.workedSolution: The labels are areas, so $60 : 135 = 4 : 9$ is $k^2$. Taking the square root of each part, the heights are $\sqrt{4} : \sqrt{9} = 2 : 3$, as required.

commonErrors.feedback: The printed ratio has been copied back. In a *show that* part the marks live in the lines above it: the simplified area ratio, then the square root.

parts.stem:
The small carton holds 400 ml.

Work out how much the large carton holds.
hints: Cube each part of the height ratio $2 : 3$.
That gives volumes $8 : 27$.
One part is $400 \div 8$.
parts.workedSolution: Heights $2 : 3$ give volumes $2^3 : 3^3 = 8 : 27$. One part is $400 \div 8 = 50$ ml, so the large carton holds $50 \times 27 = 1350$ ml.

commonErrors.feedback: The height ratio has been used on a capacity. A capacity is a volume, so cube the ratio first.
The area ratio 4 : 9 has been used on a volume. Land on the heights, then cube.

questions.solutionProgram: ratio 60:135 = 4 : 9; heights 2 : 3; volumes 8 : 27; one part = 400/8 = 50; V = 1350

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked: two similar shapes have areas 14 cm² and 126 cm². The height of the larger shape is 27 cm. Work out the height of the smaller shape. Her working:
studentWorking: Height of the smaller shape = 27 ÷ 9 = 3 cm
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 is correct and earns its mark: 9 really is the factor linking the two areas. Line 3 then uses that area factor on a height. Areas carry $k^2$, so 9 is $k^2$, not $k$, and it has to be square-rooted before it meets a length.
correction: Height of the smaller shape = 27 ÷ 3 = 9 cm
findTheMistake.feedback: One of three marks, and one square root away from all three. This is the Summer 2024 question almost exactly: the report says the area factor was found and then divided into the length, so 15 was divided by 4 instead of by 2. Add one line — "lengths = 1 : 3" — between what you have and what you wrote.

findTheMistake.stem: Erin was asked: a container has volume 40 cm³. A similar container is made with every length 3 times as long. Work out the volume of the new container. Her working:
studentWorking: Every length is 3 times as long
So the volume is 3 times as big
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 scales the volume by the length factor. The container has grown in three directions at once: it is 3 times longer, 3 times wider and 3 times taller, so the volume is multiplied by $3 \times 3 \times 3$.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks yet, and the fix is one line. This is the Summer 2023 question: the report records that the majority of candidates simply scaled the volume by the length factor, and only the better ones multiplied by the cube. Write "volume factor = k³" before any multiplying and the method mark is safe even if the arithmetic slips.

findTheMistake.stem: Saoirse was asked: two triangles are similar. A side of 6 cm on the small triangle corresponds to a side of 14 cm on the large one. Another side of the small triangle is 9 cm. Work out the matching side of the large triangle. Her working:
studentWorking: So every side of the large triangle is 8 cm longer
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 turns a difference into a rule. Similar shapes are linked by a multiplier, not by a fixed amount added on: if every side simply gained 8 cm the angles would change and the shapes would no longer be similar. The link is $14 \div 6$.
correction: Check: 6 × 7/3 = 14, so the factor is the one the shapes actually share
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing scored yet, because the method mark is for a ratio and no ratio has appeared. The November 2024 report describes the same subtraction being used on this kind of question. One habit fixes it for good: before you touch the unknown side, write $k =$ new ÷ old and check that it is greater than 1 when the shape is growing.

prompts.prompt: A shape is enlarged by scale factor $k$. What happens to a length, to an area and to a volume?
prompts.answer: Length $\times k$, area $\times k^2$, volume $\times k^3$. One dimension, two dimensions, three dimensions.

prompts.prompt: A perimeter is made of lengths. What does an enlargement of scale factor $k$ do to it?
prompts.answer: Multiplies it by $k$, not by $k^2$. A perimeter is a sum of lengths, so it takes one factor of $k$.

prompts.prompt: You are given a ratio of areas and asked for a ratio of lengths. What do you do?
prompts.answer: Simplify the ratio, then take the square root of each part. Areas carry $k^2$, so a square root brings you back to $k$.

prompts.prompt: You are given a ratio of volumes and asked for a ratio of heights. What do you do?
prompts.answer: Take the cube root of each part. Volumes carry $k^3$. For example $1 : 64$ gives heights $1 : 4$.

prompts.prompt: What is the commonest way to lose every mark after the first on a similar-shapes question?
prompts.answer: Using the area scale factor as if it were the length scale factor. The number found from two areas is $k^2$: square-root it before it touches a length.

prompts.prompt: A solid's height is doubled. What happens to its volume, and what do most candidates write?
prompts.answer: It is multiplied by $2^3 = 8$. Most candidates double it. Every length doubles, so three factors of 2 arrive.

prompts.prompt: What exactly makes two shapes similar?
prompts.answer: Every pair of corresponding angles is equal and every pair of corresponding sides is in the same ratio. One shape is an enlargement of the other; nothing but the size changes.

prompts.prompt: Two similar solids have surface areas in the ratio $9 : 25$. What is the ratio of their volumes?
prompts.answer: $27 : 125$. Square-root to the lengths $3 : 5$, then cube. There is no direct route from areas to volumes.

prompts.prompt: In a triangle $ABC$ with $DE$ parallel to $BC$, $D$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$: which side of the large triangle corresponds to $AD$?
prompts.answer: $AB$, the whole side. $DB$ is only the part left over. Add $AD$ and $DB$ first, then divide.

prompts.prompt: A 4-mark part gives two areas and two heights written as $x$ and $x + 10$, and says to show the working clearly. You can see the answer. What do you write?
prompts.answer: The area ratio simplified, the length ratio after the square root, the equation, then the value. A correct answer with no working scores nothing when the working is demanded.

findings.asked: Volume of a similar shape when the height is doubled.
findings.wentWrong: Most doubled the volume; only the better candidates multiplied by 8.
findings.rule: Length x2 means volume x2 cubed = x8.

findings.asked: Link an area scale factor to a length scale factor.
findings.wentWrong: Over 40% made the connection; many treated the area factor as the length factor.
findings.rule: Length factor = square root of the area factor.

findings.asked: Use a ratio of areas (24:96) to find a length.
findings.wentWrong: The factor 4 was found and often used directly on the length (15 / 4) instead of the length factor 2; some divided 96 by 15.
Most used the ratio of sides; a few used Pythagoras; some subtracted (10 - 4 = 6, so 15 - 6).
findings.rule: Similar shapes scale by multiplying, not by adding a difference.

findings.asked: Effect of an enlargement on perimeter and on area.
findings.wentWrong: Some gave 5 for both, showing no distinction between length and area; 10 was a common wrong area answer.
findings.rule: Perimeter scales by k, area by k squared.

findings.asked: From an area ratio of 1:16 find a height ratio and an unknown.
findings.wentWrong: Very few got x = 3; one mark for 1:16 was common, but the step to heights 1:4 was rarely made - a topic candidates seemed not to know.
findings.rule: Square-root an area ratio to get the length ratio, then use it.

findings.asked: Length and area ratios in a pair of similar shapes.
findings.wentWrong: Just over a quarter evaluated x; a few wrote the right answer with no working and got nothing.
findings.rule: Show the ratio chain: area ratio, root, length ratio, equation.

findings.asked: Ratio of heights and of volumes of cylinders given the ratio of their areas.
findings.wentWrong: Only stronger candidates continued from the area ratio to heights and volumes.
findings.rule: Area ratio to length ratio (root), then length ratio to volume ratio (cube).

insight.ruleToRemember: Length factor k, area factor k squared, volume factor k cubed; always go back to k (square root or cube root) before converting between them, and show the chain.
insight.aStarSignal: Moving from an area ratio through the length ratio to a volume ratio, with the roots and cubes written explicitly.
